doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: Making students learn a hundred tunes
summary: He assigns many standards, Bird and Monk tunes, since knowing them has paid off in work.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you require them to memorize a certain number of standards?

Yeah. I’m kind of a numbers guy. I like my students to know a lot of tunes. I shoot for a hundred. And that’s a lot. And some of my colleagues say that seems like a — but I’ve learned, as a horn player, when you know some obscure Monk tune and somebody calls their favorite Monk tune and you know it, you’re in the club. And so it really pays off to know, not just harmonies but like — like you might know eight “I Got Rhythm” tunes. But if a guy wants to play “Moose the Mooche” then you’ve got to know the head to “Moose the Mooche.” You know? And especially Bird tunes and Monk tunes. I’m a real — I’m very strict about it and I bug my students to really get in there and learn those. Because it’s really paid off for me in terms of work. So yeah, and plus they need to learn how to learn those tunes. Because when they go and learn hard original tunes they’re going to have to play them and they’re going to have to know how to learn them. And I think they learn how to learn that by learning standards. And these kids are smart and they really learn fast. I’ve got a kid at Eastman now, Christian Crawford is his name. And I assigned that Bird tune “Quasimodo,” which is a tune on “Embraceable You.” He learned it in a week. That tune took me a month to learn that tune and I was really working on it. He learned it in a week. So they know that’s just my thing. But the long answer to your question, yes I really require them learning tunes. A lot of standards. And not just the regular ones.
